10:50 (right picture) this is how I sat when I was being interview by 4 people in my current job, I usually sit like this when I feel like im going to be scrutinized so instead of stressing about doing "the perfect thing", I realized I could only be myself comfortably and that if they didn't accept me for who I am in my most relaxed human state that I shouldn't work there in the first place.  Its like a filtering mechanism, you are most happy when you are yourself and when you are relaxed, so if you want to be happy you do it by being honest to yourself, pretending to be someone you're not is dishonesty to self and others and it will only lead to misery. I changed because I realized I had no other choice, it wasn't rational for me to bury my true self and replace it with feelings of fear.   Later i was told by 2 of the interviewers that the "interview" seemed more like a conversation, I was speaking to them without fear, I showed vulnerability while 4 people were looking at me writing stuff down on paper. In school you are taught how one "should pick up the phone" what sentence structures to use to be deemed "professional" how one should compose letters etc... Most of my fear when using the phone came from trying to abide by fixed rules of phone interaction which I didn't want to "get wrong" whatever that is.  I erased this fear by realizing that the person on the other side of the line is exactly like me, they have fears, they have a family they have dreams, they are vulnerable, they are ultimately human, what they are not is "a manager", "a receptionist", "a service worker at a restaurant", these labels are people's functions in society they are not reality. I talk to these people like I would talk to a friend, my language is not official, I'm not afraid of talking to them in human terms "well what do you think I should do then?" you show vulnerability and you show trust in the person, you show that you value their opinion, and the person on the other end of the line will warm up to you on a human level. These interactions are priceless human moments.  Sometimes I'll get someone on the phone who talks very officially, usually a younger person recently employed and "well trained", they don't treat me like a human, they go by their training and talk to me like a "customer", but the funny thing is that if you talk to them straight and don't participate in their little sterile interaction they start adapting to you because you make them realize that it feels far better to talk on a more personal level and to treat each others more like friends than caricatures of corporate society.

The Jallianwala Bagh massacre, also known as the Amritsar massacre, took place on 13 April 1919 when troops of the British Indian Army under the command of Colonel Reginald Dyer fired rifles into a crowd of Indians, who had gathered in Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, Punjab. The civilians had assembled to condemn the arrest and deportation of two national leaders, Satya Pal and Saifuddin Kitchlew. There has been much debate over whether the crowd knew of the proclamation Dyer had made banning meetings, in its supposed inefficacy, however, Raja Ram has argued that the crowd formed in deliberate defiance, being the beginning of Indian nationalism.[2]  The Jallianwalla Bagh is a public garden of 6 to 7 acres (28,000 m2), walled on all sides, with five entrances.[3] To enter, troops first blocked the entry by a tank and locked the exit. On Dyer's orders, his troops fired on the crowd for ten minutes, directing their bullets largely towards the few open gates through which people were trying to flee. Official British Indian sources gave a figure of 379 identified dead,[4] with approximately 1,100 wounded. The casualty number estimated by the Indian National Congress was more than 1,500 injured, with approximately 1,000 dead.[5] This "brutality stunned the entire nation",[6] resulting in a "wrenching loss of faith" of the general public in the intentions of the UK.[7] The ineffective inquiry and the initial accolades for Dyer by the House of Lords fuelled widespread anger, leading to the Non-cooperation Movement of 1920–22.[8]  On Sunday, 13 April 1919, Dyer was convinced of a major insurrection and he banned all meetings; however this notice was not widely disseminated. That was the day of Baisakhi, the main Sikh festival, and many villagers had gathered in the Bagh. On hearing that a meeting had assembled at Jallianwala Bagh, Dyer went with Sikh, Gurkha, Baluchi, Rajput troops from 2-9th Gurkhas, the 54th Sikhs and the 59th Sind Rifles[9] to a raised bank and ordered them to shoot at the crowd. Dyer continued the firing for about ten minutes, until the ammunition supply was almost exhausted. Dyer stated that 1,650 rounds had been fired, a number apparently derived by counting empty cartridge cases picked up by the troops.[10]  Dyer was initially lauded by conservative forces in the empire, but in July 1920 he was censured and forced to retire by the House of Commons.[11] He became a celebrated hero in the UK among most of the people connected to the British Raj,[12] for example, the House of Lords,[13] but unpopular in the House of Commons, which voted against Dyer as a Colonel. He was disciplined by being removed from his appointment, was passed over for promotion and was prohibited from further employment in India.[14][15] Upon his death Rudyard Kipling declared that Dyer 'did his duty as he saw it'.[16] The massacre some historians have argued caused a re-evaluation of the army's role, in which the new policy became minimum force, however, later British actions during the Mau Mau insurgencies have led Huw Bennett to question this school of thought.[17] The army was retrained and developed less violent tactics for crowd control.[18] Some historians consider the episode a decisive step towards the end of British rule in India.[19] At 9:00 on the morning of 13 April, the traditional festival of Baisakhi, Colonel Reginald Dyer, the acting military commander for Amritsar and its environs, proceeded through the city with several city officials, announcing the implementation of a pass system to enter or leave Amritsar, a curfew beginning at 20:00 that night and a ban on all processions and public meetings of four or more persons. The proclamation was read and explained in English, Urdu, Hindi and Punjabi, but few paid it any heed or appear to have learned of it later.[40] Meanwhile, the local CID had received intelligence of the planned meeting in the Jallianwala Bagh through word of mouth and plainclothes detectives in the crowds. At 12:40, Dyer was informed of the meeting and returned to his base at around 13:30 to decide how to handle it.[41]  By mid-afternoon, thousands of Sikhs, Muslims and Hindus had gathered in the Jallianwala Bagh (garden) near the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. Many who were present had earlier worshipped at the Golden Temple, and were passing through the Bagh on their way home. The Bagh was (and is) an open area of six to seven acres, roughly 200 yards by 200 yards in size, and surrounded by walls roughly 10 feet in height. Balconies of houses three to four stories tall overlooked the Bagh, and five narrow entrances opened onto it, several with locked gates. During the rainy season, it was planted with crops, but served as a local meeting-area and playground for much of the year.[42] In the center of the Bagh was a samadhi (cremation site) and a large well partly filled with water which measured about 20 feet in diameter.[42]  Apart from pilgrims, Amritsar had filled up over the preceding days with farmers, traders and merchants attending the annual Baisakhi horse and cattle fair. The city police closed the fair at 14:00 that afternoon, resulting in a large number of people drifting into the Jallianwala Bagh. It was estimated that about 20,000 to 25,000 people had gathered in the Bagh by the time of the meeting. Dyer sent an aeroplane to overfly the Bagh and estimate the size of the crowd.[42] By this time, both Colonel Dyer and Deputy Commissioner Irving, the senior civil authority for Amritsar, were well aware of the meeting, but took no actions to prevent it or send police to peacefully disperse the crowds. This would later be a serious criticism levelled at both Dyer and Irving.  An hour after the meeting began as scheduled at 16:30, Colonel Dyer arrived at the Bagh with a group of ninety Sikh, Gurkha, Baluchi (note that the Baluch Regiment of the British Indian Army did not have Baluch troops, the British having failed in their efforts to get the Baluch to enlist and serve; the Baluch continued to fight an insurgency of varying intensity with the British from 1839 to 1947. The Baluch regiment was staffed by troops from the Punjab and other areas of India), Rajput from 2-9th Gurkhas, the 54th Sikhs and the 59th Sind Rifles soldiers.[9] Fifty of them were armed with .303 Lee–Enfield bolt-action rifles. It is not clear whether Dyer had specifically chosen troops from that ethnic group due to their proven loyalty to the British or that they were simply the Sikh and non-Sikh units most readily available. He had also brought two armored cars armed with machine guns; however, the vehicles were left outside, as they were unable to enter the Bagh through the narrow entrances. The Jallianwala Bagh was surrounded on all sides by houses and buildings and had few narrow entrances. Most of them were kept permanently locked. The main entrance was relatively wide, but was guarded heavily by the troops backed by the armoured vehicles.  Dyer—without warning the crowd to disperse—blocked the main exits. He 'explained' later that this act "was not to disperse the meeting but to punish the Indians for disobedience."[43]Dyer ordered his troops to begin shooting toward the densest sections of the crowd. This abuse story really hits close to home for me. I dealt with a lot of verbal and psychological (occasionally physical) abuse from my mother and her parents when I had to live at their house after my parents got divorced. My experience was very similar, with the exception that none of it was being filmed for money.   At the time I thought it was totally normal. It was hard to focus on the bad things when I was constantly showered with toys and all other kinds of gifts that I hadn't even asked for (later on I would be screamed at for being a spoiled brat because of all the things I was given). I was about 13 when this started, and I got out of it when I was 15 once my mother was convinced to leave their house while my grandfather was out of state on a business trip. I remember my grandmother yelling curses at us from the top of the stairs as we packed our most important belongings with help from my aunt.   I had a therapist legally forced on me at the time of my parents' divorce whom I honestly disliked from the moment I met her. Talking to her felt very unnatural and uncomfortable. I didn't and still don't think I needed therapy at that time, nor do I think I need it now. I'm the type of person to deal with these sorts of issues on my own with my own reasoning skills. As the sessions went on, I only had less and less to talk about. By the time I was nearing the end of my sessions, I would simply walk into her office and say "I have nothing to talk about." while the next 30 minutes was spent sitting in silence. The abuse at home I did talk about at first, but I know the way I talked about it was pretty nonchalant and tended to downplay the actual situation. At the time I was overwhelmed by all the legal intervention as at this point, I was only allowed to see my father once a week which was pretty devastating for me since I'd always had a very strong, close relationship with him. I new that if I spoke completely candidly about what was going on, I could be removed from my mother's custody which sounds good on the surface considering the abuse; however, it would have ultimately made the situation worse as my father had no chance at getting custody either because he'd had drug problems in the past, though he'd never been violent or in any way a danger to anyone.  My initial feeling about my therapist proved to be warranted as I later found out that she had been feeding any and all information I gave her to my grandfather who was the major instigator of the abuse (he is also suspected of being a pedophile and had apparently asked my mother for sexual favors while we were both living there. I also want to note that he was my mother's stepfather and not biologically related).   At this stage, maybe a month or 2 before we eventually left, I was really getting scared and desperate, so after I went out to the backyard, I called some of my friends from school and asked them for advice. They were also around the same age as me, so they weren't exactly the biggest help, though they did provide moral support and gave me the push I needed to do what I did next. I had an idea of what I wanted to do, but I lastly called my father to confirm that what I was about to do was a good idea. I then began walking quickly to a nearby park and recreational center because I didn't want my abusers around to control the situation.   When I got to the park it was about 10:00 at night. I took out my phone and called 911 and informed them of my location and that I was afraid of the members of my household. The operator informed me that they'd sent a car out and hung up, but I was still afraid of standing there by myself and was certain that my grandfather would find me soon, so I called my father's mother whom I currently live with along with my father and stepmother. She met me at the park and I ended up sitting in the car with her while we waited for the police. She had already known about the whole situation and was also very afraid for me. By the time the police showed up I was shaking and it seemed everything I needed to recount to the officer had totally left my brain. I did my best to ramble out everything that I could think of in between sobs as I'd started to cry halfway through my statement out of fear and general anxiety about what was going on. My good grandmother did best to fill in the gaps and provide information where she could.   The officer was a younger man who seemed very understanding and sympathetic. A few minutes later, another police car showed up (I later found out that the second officer was called in response to my grandfather having noticed my absence). The second officer was a woman who seemed a bit older than the other guy and was apparently his superior. I did my best to tell her the same things I told the male officer, but it was obvious that she didn't believe me, nor did she seem to care about my very real and immediate fear. I think the male officer tried to explain it to her, but she wasn't having any of it for whatever reason, and decided that I had just run away from home for shits and giggles. She wasted no time in putting me into the back of her police car and driving me back to my abusers.  When we got there, she spoke to my grandfather and laid out all the possible charges that could be pressed against me. He convinced my mother to go along with it, and I felt utterly defeated and totally helpless. After the stunt I pulled, the abuse was no longer sugarcoated with excuses and gifts but was instead openly hostile and malicious. I was lucky that it didn't last much longer.   After my mother and I had moved to a safe place, we had the legal charges against me dropped, and everything was much more peaceful. At that time, my time with my father was still limited, but with my abusive grandparents out of the picture, it was pretty easy to sneak extra time with him under my mother's nose by having him pick me up at the school bus stop before the bus came and skip that school day to spend the day with him. By the time I turned 16, there was really no way for her to keep me with her, so I packed my things and told her I was going to live with my dad. Everything has been okay since then. I still deal with a lot of anxiety and some minor OCD and have trouble getting out of the house to do things, but my psychological trauma has been kept to a minimum, which makes me feel very lucky. I have visited Japan twice now, once last summer 2016 and just now Dec. 2017.  Yes, there are definitely things that are expensive especially in Tokyo but boy, you also have lots of cheap options.  This video is really good but I just want to clarify some things and/or add info.  The Tokyo subway is vast and is operated by multiple different lines (private and government).  One is a private company which is Japan Rail who also operate the Shinkansen.  You can only get the Japan Rail pass outside of Japan as a tourist and is definitely worth it.  Like the video says, it only takes one long ride on the Shinkansen to make the 1 week pass worth it and on top of that you can ride the Japan Rail trains in the city for free.  BUT, here is the clarification, JR is not the metro/subway, it is only a portion of it.  There is a massive network of trains.  If you ONLY got the JR pass, you cannot ride the rest of the subway system in Tokyo.  You can only ride on the trains operated by JR.  Now the video is wrong in that it says you have to stand around buying tickets if you don't get the JR pass.  That's also not true.  What you should do is to buy a PASMO or SUICA card.  These are literally train debit cards and they work across all these different train companies.  They come preloaded with amounts and you can just tap your way through all the trains and it will deduct an amount each time.  No need to go buy a ticket each time and figure out how much it costs.  When the balance runs low (and you'll see your balance every time you tap),  you can just re-charge them in the ticket machines.  I got mine from Haneda airport and when I left I just returned it at the airport and I got a 500 Yen deposit refund for the card.  Concerning the food, I would definitely pick Yoshinoya over the other ones.  I find its quality just a bit better and the prices just as good.  But I had a lunch at Nakajima in Shinjuku and it is a 1 Michelin Star restaurant.  Guess how much the lunch is:  800 Yen!  So how's that for a budget lunch at a 1 Michelin star restaurant.  It opens at 11:30am so lineup early.  I waited just short of an hour but if you get there like 11:30am your wait should be shorter.  There is also a 1 Michelin star ramen place in Tokyo (near Sengoku) and cheapest ramen is 1000 Yen, its name is Tsuta.  And there are many other top notch ramen shops whose prices are cheaper too.  I also find 7 Eleven, Lawson, Family Mart to be full of good stuff to buy but you can try their local grocery stores and they have even MORE items with the same prices.  And the food shops in the train stations are amazing and tons of selection with excellent prices.  I also agree with the video's recommendation of business hotel.  I got one last year and it slept 3 of us plenty well with a kitchen/dining table too and it was just a bit higher than the capsule hotel prices.  Happy travels in Japan!

At around 25:00, he says that there are an infinite ways of construing the world, but only a limited number of ways with which one can successfully live and interact in the world.  It hit me that the same is true with regard to food.  We can come up with an infinite number of dietary plans or ways of eating, but there truly are only a limited number of ones which will sustain human health generation after generation.  For instance, when human diets were researched almost 100 years ago, there was a wide variety, ranging from insects/nuts/fish on tropical islands to oil/fat/meat in the arctic, but all the diets still met certain narrow principles (A/D consumption from animal foods, fermenting grains/nuts/dairy, broth, salt, sea food, etc.).  No groups were vegan, for instance.  I suppose after hundreds of thousands of years, you sort of figure out what doesn't keep a population thriving long-term.    And (thinking aloud) we sort of threw it all out in the 20th century.  Progress at all costs, I guess.  Maybe there's wisdom in listening to the "democracy of the past"?  We now imagine we can eat any way, live any way, marry any way, raise children any way, and it will all work out.  Maybe it magically will, or maybe, as always, nature will select the fittest and the rest will die off, either with bad health or tribal warfare.

47:40 I'm a little disappointed with the guest's conflation of gravitational force and gravitational potential. If you had a planet with a large twin that it was tidally locked with, yes, it would shape itself to have a uniform gravitational potential, but that is not equivalent to having the same surface gravity everywhere. The force due to gravity is proportional to the gradient of the gravitational potential, and just because the potential may be the same everywhere along the surface, it doesn't mean the gradient is the same everywhere.  Similarly, the situation with super-earths isn't so much that the surface gravity is so high, but that with a more massive planet, you are likely to be too deep in the gravitational well to be able to escape. You could have, for example, a planet with twice the radius of the Earth and four times the mass. The gravitational acceleration, -G*M/R^2, is the same as on Earth, because -G*M/R^2 == -G*(4M)/(2R)^2. But the gravitational potential, -G*M/R (not squared!) is much lower (i.e., a larger negative number) for the super-earth, so even though you could launch a rocket, and it would look similar to launching it from Earth, you wouldn't be able to burn the engines long enough to climb out of the potential well.  (Source: my masters thesis)

36:20 How to Make Gourmet Krispy Kreme Doughnuts  Base dough:  30 oz. all purpose flour  0.5 oz kosher salt  2 oz honey  1 packet active dry yeast  4 oz unsalted butter cut into small pieces  Liquid mixture:  4 oz. egg (2 large eggs)  2 oz. honey  1 oz vegetable oil  1 tbsp vanilla extract  16 oz. tepid whole milk  In the bowl of a large stand mixer w/ a dough hook, combine all base dough ingredients. Make a well in the center of the bowl. Whisk liquid mixture ingredients together in a separate bowl. Pour the mixture into the well and mix on low until a shaggy dough forms. Increase speed and continue mixing until dough is smooth, supple, and no longer sticky. Gather the dough into a ball, flour all over, and place into a clean bowl, covered. Let it sit at room temperature until nearly doubled in size, then transfer bowl to refrigerator and chill until cold (preferably overnight). Scrape the dough onto a floured surface. Working quickly and flouring as needed to prevent sticking, roll out to 1/2" thickness. Use two circle cutters to punch out 3 1/4" donuts, with 1 1/4" cutout, fitting them as closely as possible to maximize yield. Arrange donut on its own square of parchment paper and allowed to proof at room temperature until puffed (could be as soon as 10 minutes).  Fill a dutch oven 1/3 of the way up with neutral oil (e.g. vegetable oil) and heat to 325°F. Working in batches, fry the donuts, turning once, until they're golden brown all over except for a pale ring around the sides (3-4 minutes). Let cool on a wire rack.  Glaze:  600 grams powdered sugar  Pinch of kosher salt  2 tsps. vanilla extract  30 grams refined coconut oil  150 grams whole milk  Whisk until smooth.  Pour slowly over cold donuts, covering completely. Let glaze set at room temperature.

0:28 "A black hole appears when an extraordinary amount of matter"  Nope. You dont need extraordinary amounts of matter to form a black hole. You simply need any amount X of matter compressed below its Schwarzchild radius.  0:48 "If you were to fall into a black hole nothing bad would happen until you crossed the event horizon" That depends on the mass of the black hole. That statement is true for supermassive black holes without accretion disks (if there was a disk, it would vaporize you well before you ever got close to the horizon). If the BH is small enough (< 30 solar masses), you will get spaghettified before reaching the event horizon. That is bad news for your survival. The smaller the BH, the faster you die before reaching the horizon.  Also this video is very simplified. If youre interested in getting to the hairy details, including hairy black holes (thats a real thing), you should check out PBS Spacetime and Sixty Symbol videos on BH's.

Perhaps the most beautiful and underrated aspect of this second appearance by Randall Carlson is how thoughtfully crafted each discussion is. Clearly this man is a brilliant educator, because he says something at the 1:16:00 mark that almost blew right past me. He's demonstrating to Joe what the Bering Land Bridge looked like and in the process mentions Atlantis, but rather than draw that out into a separate discussion he just goes; "We talked about that last time, but... ".  I know this seems like a minor thing, but one of the issues I have with repeat guests on podcasts is that they almost always come with repeat stories. If you listen to both episodes with Paul Stamets, for example, you'll very quickly realize that these are basically the same episode repeated over two separate appearances. Whether this is because the guest is unsure what he's already told Joe or because he really only has a podcast's worth of information to his name, we may never know. What we do know, though, is that for any listeners paying serious attention to these episodes (which many do) these rehashed conversations can be incredibly wearing.  No disrespect to Graham Hancock, because he's one of my absolute favorite guests, but even he is guilty of repeating certain stories or nuggets of information every single time he appears on the podcast. What I'm noticing from Randall Carlson, though, is that his first two appearances are not only entirely different, but the second is an almost perfect compliment to the first. It makes me wonder if Randall didn't listen to his first appearance before recording his second just to avoid repeating himself, because his knowledge of what had already been said is practically flawless.  Not only does this make him an excellent guest and friend to Joe Rogan, but it makes him a truly special educator. That kind of attention to detail is rare, and it only enhances his credibility as a scientist to have so much of this subject in order. This is clearly a man who cares very much about his work and it shows a great deal of integrity that he comes so prepared. It's because he's this disciplined that he's able to make such a complicated subject so easy to understand. In my opinion, that really is the mark of a true genius. I suppose that's why this video is nearing the 10 million views mark and counting.   And credit to Joe for giving him such a platform! His ability to just sit and listen, and only chime in when there's a pertinent question to be asked, absolutely contributes to the specialness of these episodes. He really does do a brilliant job making Randall look good. When it comes to podcast hosts, from a listener's perspective, that's all you can ask for!

On the note and the topic of the podcast - as a psychologist, I've sensed a lot of emotions coming from Mo during this time, but I'm also partial to take the conjecture for granted. He's got a brilliant mind, and he's a massive expert in his field, but speaking about human connection and how AI can, or will be able to replicate it is nothing more but wishful thinking which I belive has it's roots in Mo's personal experience regarding the loss of his son, seems my hunch was right [USER]:01 when he projects his son who had passed away onto a machine.   Without knowing, he literally showed how he's already hoping technology could in part fill the hole in his heart regarding his son. But replicating human connection is truly only possible if one falls into a trap of delusion, and subconsciously ignores the fact that it's a program on the other end. You can't replicate a mother's womb, you can't replicate the act of feeding a baby on a tit, you can't replicate mothers warm embrace. Even step-parents can't fill a gaping hole in a soul of a child left by its parents upon birth - even if they don't remember it. It's well documented and backed by facts.   So based on the knowledge in how the human mind, and connection works, no, AI won't ever be able to replace human connection. It will be able to simulate it, maybe even extremely well, but never replicate the original. There's plenty of studies and data available that back this up. Even real humans can't replace biological parents who are not there anymore, there's been an extensive research on this topic.   Now will it try to simulate? Yes. What will the effects be? Who knows, but none that are helpful to humans. They will all be designed to give instant gratification with 0 effort, further fueling the depression and anxiety we see in modern society. That may or may not lead to tighter regulation, but one thing is for sure - we'll need an army of psychologists in the upcoming decades, and may God help us all.   So due to the experiences that Mo had had during his life, and mainly his losses, I believe he's got a subconscious vested interest in believing that AI will be able to achieve this.   But as a psychologist I guarantee you that evething regarding human connection in this podcast is pure guesswork, based on their own personal beliefs of how connection and humans work, which is not at all how our minds actually work. So just be careful of not falling into a trap of taking their opinions as your own. Do research, and find out for yourself. In a way, this video sounds like my life story. The parts where I fear to admit. The fear to to tell others. The terrible feeling that anchors and weights in, by just simply acknowledging and thus making it into a topic that will define the new me... A blind cripple. They even showed the same visual deterioration, associated with sever cloudy vision ( 4:54 ). But there were differences.   The differences was that in my time span of slowly going blind (6 years): 5 family members passed away where I witnessed 3 of their funerals, my grandparents of both sides decided to bid their farewell along with my oldest uncle. My older sister was diagnosed with breast cancer, while my younger sis was going through her divorce and raising the mess of a child the, terrible father, left us with (she and her child lives with us). And my Ma discovering my father was cheating on her years~ ago, where upon him, he had put an end with it- when I was born.   Now, I'm 27, went through a surgery  to remove the Cataracts in both my eyes. I ended up with 20/20 vision, which I now can finally SEE! (with details!)  My sister survived her chemo treatment, somewhat scarred, and is cancer free. My younger sister overcame her divorce, found a new man, and conceived a beautiful beautiful baby girl while her bf ( the soon the be newly weds) step forward and laid down the, empty, fatherly (TOUGH) love my unruly nephew can only respond to. And lastly my ma forgave my dad, but not forget.  "Life is like roller coaster". I believe I've read that in a children's book, long ago?   It only took me 6 years to understand the only thing separating an adolescent and an adult is surviving the experience of loss, pain, and sorrow of life, Where everyone would inevitably and forcefully have to face through.  Take upon my story which-ever way you will, because as awful as things were headed it will get better.   -And that is my victory. Great video. I'm in the middle of making it now. Some first timer experience: A) Even if you intend to make only one loaf and wanna half the quantities - do not! Half the dough is going to be wasted because it sticks to anything that it touches, so the final  dough that stays in one peace is quite small. B) Prepare two poolishes - it takes long and if you decide to retry after all the dough got wasted/washed off your hands, you want another poolish ready right away. C) the stage where the dough is being picked up at 03:33 is harder than it looks, you try to pick it and it just pulls and tears and a lot gets stuck to the hand. More flour and some more folds allowed forming a pickable piece. And the time that it takes to pull-fold and then pick-rotate-flip-drop - 30 minutes while in the video it looks like a single minute. D) Since i was so slow on the previous stage, should i still let the dough rest the same time before the second folding? E)  Wetting the hands too many times or doing it after there is already much dough stuck to your hands - causes the dough to become moist and more sticky. F) The stage where you pull the sides and tuck below - do not pull too tight or it will tear on top or on the side. And then - remixing, refolding an retucking. Another half an hour. And a dough of kinda wrong consistensy because of all the flour that it picked from the work surface. G) Liberately flouring - do not be too liberal or it will cause the crust be covered under flour and you won't know what color it even is. H) A towel instead of gloves is not enough with the dutch oven. There IS moisture inside it - it's invisible. 250 degrees C is A LOT hotter than the usual 150-170 that most dishes cook at, so there is not even a trace of vapor condensate - just surprisingly hot steamy air. I) When you scar the loaf - pay at least some attention to the shape, so that you do not get an unintentional swastika or zeta symbol. K) Overall - nice, thick crunchy crust. My wife really liked the bread.

It's not that eyewitness testimony is useless... It's that some witnesses are drastically less useful than others in regards to their powers of observation and their individual susceptibility to their memories being manipulated either by their own minds or by various social pressures.  The guy at 1:08:27 is a fantastic example of someone who may not have the best powers of observation, but who did not yield to internal or external pressures when being questioned about something that they know they did not observe well.  Most people, when asked so many times about the package, would have begun filling in details about it, based on guesses from their memory. 2:50: It is actually incorrect when you say that monthly income dividend does not pay you more. When you are paid monthly, you can re-invest that money each month which would snowball your growth faster if you re-invest those dividends each month (as opposed to quarterly). Whether that company is fundamentally strong is another story but purely from a frequency standpoint, more payments do equal more payment as time goes on (assuming you are re-investing the dividends) but that argument could be said for the same thing if you were re-investing quarterly companies.    This is also why fractional shares are so powerful. It makes your fractional shares squeeze even more juice out of the stock versus having to wait until you have enough for a full share only.   Lets use an example to make it simple If I have 1 stock that is $10 and yields 4%. That means you get $0.10 per quarter. Or I make 0.0033 per month if it pays monthly In a monthly payment, I would have 0.0033c which I can use fractionally shares to buy more shares. Now I own 1.00033 shares of the stock by the next month which means I would receive more dividends, 0.0034c next month. Then next month, I make 0.0035c per month. By the time you receive your quarterly dividend, I already have 0.00035 more of a share than you. These are small numbers because the stock is $10 but if the stock is $50+ and you have $10,000+ in the position, you can see how much more it amplifies. Then you add 5-10 years of compound interest, it will be insane. As you can see, even after 2-3 years, I would be way farther ahead than you in terms of position size.   As I said, this assumes a couple of things. A) You are able to buy fractional shares but assuming you had a large enough position, the fractional shares wouldn't matter. B) The company fundamentally is strong which I agree that finding a strong monthly company is it's own battle.

From a former US Navy Recruiter:  To get a Navy Challenge contract (SEALs, EOD, SWCC, Navy Diver), you need to do at least 75 push-ups and 75 sit-ups. Most SOF guys will tell you that you aren't really competitive unless you can do at least 100 of each. You actually failed the pull-ups section of the test because you need to perform the pull-up with your hands facing away. Challenge PST observers would have scored you both zero on your pull-ups. To get a Challenge contract a person needs to do 15 pull-ups. I'm sure you both know you need to work on running and swimming, but a Challenge contract requires times of less than 9:30 in each. Also, don't swim with shoes on. To actually get through BUD/S, SEALs recommend that you show up being able to swim 500 yards in under 8:00, at least 100 push-ups and sit-ups, at least 20 pull-ups, and be able to run 1.5 miles in less than 8:00. Once you hit those numbers, focus on running longer distances and doing swim workouts with fins. Fins do make you go faster, but if you swim for the same time in fins, until you're used to them, your calves will be on fire. According to Stew Smith who studies the physical statistics of those who make it through BUD/S, the better you are at running, the more likely you are to make it through BUD/S.

Hey guys, I’ve taken about 7 or 8 PSTs in the last year, passed all of them and received a Navy rescue swimmer contract. So here is my $.2. This is just for anyone wondering, not to be a YouTube troll. Good on you guys for trying. These are called PST(physical screening test) and are done by all spec op/war candidates to earn a contract.   Swim- in my opinion the swim always warmed up my shoulders and body in general. Going cold into push ups and pull ups is rough. Also, I don’t remember if Seals can do breast stroke, but they mostly use combat side stroke. Rescue swimmers have to do freestyle. You guys did some sort breast stroke thing. Breast stroke is a great stroke and relaxing, but not the fastest. The major difference is that you’re doing it in a pool and can push off the walls which helps a lot. It also helps keep you in a straight line. If you zigzag around, you just swim more. You also had 10 minutes to change and with demonstrations probably a 15 minute rest after the swim.   Pushups- solid form, def keep your eyes up. PRO TIP: sort of twisting your hand into the ground will turn your elbows closer/into your torso and facing more directly behind you. Forearm facing toward. In turn you will use the bigger muscles in your chest and overtime will be able to get really good numbers. When your elbows are bowed out in the down position you use a lot of shoulder and no matter what will tire out faster. 60 ish push ups mostly as far as you will get with your elbows out. To get those 80-100 numbers get that elbow in.   Sit ups- arms across chest and hands on the collar bones. Over the knee was definitely extra. We did maybe 2 Inches below the knee.   Pull ups- hands forward. Aside from that, they were solid looking.   Run- 10:50 isn’t a bad time. 10:15 was auto qual for RS. Not sure about SO.   If you guys are ever in San Diego, ca let me know if you want to do something on base. Cheers.

Ok so like this is really resonating because when I was in high school I was probably my theatre director’s favorite male actor, aside from the one who played the hero, while I was cast as the villain. If I auditioned, I was pretty much always in the show, partly because of my really good relationship with the director, but also just because I worked to develop my skills. I was really good at singing and acting because I worked really hard at it, and held a high standard for myself. I’m fully aware this makes me sound like a douchebag, but I’ve wasted too much of my life apologizing for myself lol  The thing that sucks about success and envy that Natalie managed to 360 no-scope is that I got such weird treatment from other theatre kids, especially the older ones. It was always passive aggressive quips and “you’re the favorite”. It always had such a venomous edge to it, and I’m recognizing now what that was. Since I had succeeded in winning the directors favor through building a relationship and honing my skills (i.e. working hard), I didn’t deserve the roles that I got because I was her favorite. It completely invalidated my accomplishments, and made them my fault somehow. And no one wanted to be my friend, even when I did my best to impress everybody so maybe they would like me.   So, yeah, being envied sucks. It’s the worst, because there’s nothing you can do to appease it aside from giving up what you have. And I ended up, you guessed it, apologizing for myself constantly and more or less being a total doormat to the older kids, and seeing myself as unworthy. Even when I succeeded I was still stuck in a really toxic mental state, in a way. Trying not to do that anymore, and after this video, I’m feeling reaffirmed in that. I hate that America (maybe other places too, just speaking from my own experience) promotes envy in such a way, because it really does poison everybody involved.  Anyways. 3:30 AM thoughts.

Way too broad - little actionable information in this. Let's talk about the two major types of brands: corporate/organizational and product/service specific. I say "organizational" bcz there are many non-profits, churches, etc. that brand their services despite not intending to generate a profit. They have THEIR clientele, clients, patients, etc. and their need to attract and maintain them in order to continue to reach their goals from a warm meal to a homeless person to (possibly) saving that person's soul. Coke is an organizational brand; diet Coke is also a brand. Rule #1: no branded product or service shall damage the corporate brand. For example, Bud Light vs Anheiser Busch. No-no-no ... !  Basically IMO, a brand is an expectation of ... typically ... a level of quality, service, reliability, etc. There's an almost limitless number of product/service attributes a potential customer/client could look for a brand to contain, but marketing has to focus-down onto a few - the few that the marketer believes to best represent as the primary target for his/her product/service at a price-point that is sustainable (it could be a break-even for a non-profit, or even an outright loss for other humanitarian organizations that draw their funds and support from outside parties such as churches or the UN).   For Diet Coke, for example, those could be: flavor (as close to "real" Coke as possible given an artificial sweetener), carbonation level, quantity (12 oz, 3 ltr, etc. vs a 55 gal drum), availability, cost/potential sale price, packaging (durability vs visual appeal), and a few others. The important thing here is -THESE ARE ALL ACTIONABLE ITEMS OR ASPECTS OF THE PRODUCT/SERVICE. People can and do manipulate these factors into a successful product/service. Millions of different brands (one for each person who buys or considers buying a product/service)? Maybe, but they will ALL be some variation of those product/service factors. 10:59 I used to work with similar camera systems for the U.S. Army, not an ATFLIR but a POP300 which had FLIR (forward-looking infrared) cameras simlar to this one.  To me, this looks like the camera losing target lock, rather than rapid acceleration by the target.  The way these tracking systems work involves some software comparing the color of the pixels within a "targeting window" (a small portion of the screen) against its surroundings. The target window in this case is the set of two horizontal lines that are constantly changing size in the center of the screen. This window can automatically resize itself, or can be manually resized by the operator, although it's usually left in the former configuration.  Although I'm not familiar with this specific ATFLIR's on-screen telemetry data, I assume the "WA OK" tag in the bottom right of the screen stands for "window automatic OK", or something similar, and it disappears just as the object begins "moving". You can even see the window rapidly resizing as it attempts to keep a lock on the target.  Furthermore, the degrees indicator (which I think is lateral degrees from forward, where 360 degrees would be straight ahead, 358, 357, 356 would be slightly to the left, and 1, 2, 3 would be slightly to the right), the degrees indicator is counting up slowly from 6 to 8 degrees. This indicates that either the F-18 is in the middle of a heading change itself, or that the target is moving laterally relative to the F-18.  My conclusion (and take this with a grain of salt, please), is that the camera lost its target lock, indicated by the loss of the "WA OK" flag in the bottom right. I assume that the ATFLIR system would be capable of tracking a moving target under normal conditions (as that's what it's designed to do), so perhaps the constant switching of zoom levels by the operator caused the target window to "lose" the pixels it was searching for during a transition.  Edit: Under further scrutiny, the flag seems to actually read "W4 OK" rather than "WA OK". Unfortunately as I'm not familiar with this term I can only guess as what it means, but its disappearance at the same time as the object's movement suggests that my previous conclusion still holds water.

Retail banks ("consumer" banks) also have this ability and that's precisely what distinguishes them from other financial institutions such as insurance or investment firms.  However, central and retail banks create 2 different types of money. Central banks create "central" money which can only be exchanged between these retail banks. Instead, retail banks create fiduciary ("fiat") money which is used by everyone (consumers, companies etc). This money creation happens when a cresit is created. Retail banks do not need to have the funds to make a credit. Instead, money is created at that moment. When the Credit is paid back, the debt is erased and the money destroyed.   Central banks can to some extent control how retail banks create money, but they actually not have that much control (at least in the Euro zone). Last weekend I went fishing on the Rainy River which divides Minnesota and Ontario. There was an obvious divide since 99% of the boats there were on the USA side. Literally could imagine the international border between our two countries just by looking at where the boats are. Its basically an honor system because authorities barely patrol these waters. You can see this river I am talking about at 3:28 of this video. East (right) of Lake of the Woods where the northwest angle is.

In a couple of points in this video you can see a common problem that arises when using meandering rivers as the basis for political borders. While rivers make great natural borders, they don't make very good political ones because their courses change over time, especially meandering ones. When a river goes through a bend, land will be eroded from the outside of the bend where the water pushes against the bank while sediment will be deposited along the inside of the bend extending it out. These forces of erosion and deposition  mean that small bends in a river eventually become large, dramatic horseshoes, lakes, or even straight courses again given enough time. You can see it clearly at 0:06. The political border clearly once followed that river, but over time the river's course changed and now the political border appears to be doing some nonsensical bullshit that cuts land off from its own country on both sides.  Choosing to use rivers as the basis for borders is efficient and effective in the short term, but in the long term it means that you will either have to periodically redraw the borders to account for changes in the river's course, which might not be popular with people who like living in, say, Virginia more than Maryland, or you need to accept that within as little as a few decades your border might not make any sense.

She told me we are going to the doctor right now (and again really confused me didn’t know what the hell was going on). We went to the doctors office at about 8:00 PM and my mom explained what was happening. The doctor then tells me I’m getting a ultrasound on my neck where my thyroid is. I was scared at first thinking they had to stick something inside my throat, all it is is pretty much putting this warm gel on the camera and moving it to see other parts. It was very relaxing I must say. Anyways, the doctor called my parents and recommended that they take me to a ENT (ears, nose, throat) and have him check something’s out with my neck. Now I was really worried, because I’ve never been under anesthesia before and I’ve never been in a real hospital before. My ENT did the operation and when he was done he left the room and pulled my parents aside and told them that things aren’t looking to pretty… and he said “Where would you like to go for treatment I can’t do much more for your son.” I didn’t know that was going on, couple days later the news got out and I had Papillary Thyroid Cancer. My mother was in tears and I hugged her for a very long time, I wasn’t crying at all.  On 1/5/18 I arrived at the University of Chicago children’s hospital and I was operated for 12 HOURS (1 hour for pre operation, 1 for post operation, and 10 for surgery)! I was left with a huge scar from ear-to-ear and 2 drain scars (drainage from my collarbone). I had great nurses who made my day better and one nurse called me a badass! I felt so good after hearing that and made a poem about myself going through thyroid cancer! It’s about the end of the last week in January and it’s about to start February. My endocrinologist said that I have to start this low iodine diet and starve my body from iodine, I had no choice but to do it and start radioactive iodine for treatment. I was back at the University of Chicago Comers Children’s hospital again and spent the night there for my treatment. I had breakfast took a shower, couple hours later I was throwing up my life. I was pressing every single nurse or help button there was in my room and finally got a nurse to come into my room to help me. I was done throwing up, couple hours after that I became really really dizzy to the point where I passed out on my bed, I heard very high pitched noises while I was dizzy and again pressed every single help button, another nurse came to help me and took my radioactivity level, she said that I could go home and get into my room for isolation. I was so so so bored out of my mind in my own room! I even got tired of playing on my phone (shocking to me because I’m literally attached to my phone). Last day of isolation my dad was making homemade pizza, I asked for extra cheese (I couldn’t have any dairy on my low iodine diet) and I was in HEAVEN! I felt normal again after eating cheese for the first time in forever! (😂)  I have remained cancer free for 1 year and my diagnosis date is coming up soon on 12/11/2019, hopefully making that 2 years cancer free.  If you are ever going through a hard time in life, don’t worry! You will get through this! Remain positive and your family and friends always will have your back!
